opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting combinations out there right now, and I'd say it's actually a very natural fit. The thing about reinforcement learning is that it needs a signal, a reward, and the quality of what you learn is only as good as that signal. In a lot of domains the reward is fuzzy. You're asking a human, or another model, "Was that answer good?" and that's noisy and it can be gamed. Theorem provers give you something quite different: a mechanical, sound check. Either the proof goes through or it doesn't. So you get a reward signal you can actually trust, and you can generate it at enormous scale without a person in the loop.

And it works in the other direction too. For decades the hard part of automated reasoning has been search. The logic is sound, but finding the proof means navigating a huge space: which lemma to apply, which induction hypothesis to choose, how to strengthen an invariant. We've built very clever heuristics for that, but heuristics are brittle. Learned policies, trained with RL against the prover, turn out to be quite good at that kind of guidance. The neural side proposes and the symbolic side disposes. The model can be creative, even wrong a lot of the time, and that's fine, because nothing gets through unless the prover accepts it.

That's really the way I think about it at AWS. We care about getting answers that are provably correct: is this access policy doing what you think, does this cryptographic code meet its spec, does this distributed protocol preserve its invariants. Customers don't want "probably correct" for those questions. So the appeal of putting generative models and RL together with formal reasoning is that you keep the soundness guarantee while gaining much more automation. Things that used to need a PhD in formal methods spending weeks writing proofs by hand become much more tractable.

I'd add a couple of caveats. First, the proof only tells you the artifact meets the specification. It doesn't tell you the specification is what you actually wanted. So a lot of the real work, and I think the next frontier, is helping people get the specification right: turning natural language intent into formal statements, and then explaining the results back in terms people understand. Second, you have to be careful that the RL agent isn't exploiting gaps in the checker, things like trusted axioms, "sorry"-style escapes, or an unsound encoding. The reward is only trustworthy if the trusted computing base is small and well understood.

But overall I'm very optimistic. I think we're heading toward a world where much more of what gets generated, code, configurations, even reasoning in natural language, comes with a machine-checkable argument for why it's correct. Reinforcement learning against theorem provers is one of the main engines that will get us there.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think it's one of the most exciting developments in the space, honestly. For a long time, automated reasoning had this fundamental tension: the search spaces are enormous, and the tools we built, things like SAT and SMT solvers, were driven largely by hand-crafted heuristics that experts tuned over decades. They work remarkably well, but they're brittle in places, and they hit walls. What reinforcement learning brings is a way to learn those heuristics, to learn where to look in the search space, rather than having a human guess.

The thing I keep coming back to is that theorem proving is almost the ideal setting for RL. You have a perfectly reliable reward signal. Either the proof checks or it doesn't. There's no ambiguity, no need to collect human labels, no reward hacking in the usual sense, because the proof checker is the arbiter and it's tiny and trustworthy. So you can let the system explore, make mistakes, generate enormous amounts of its own training data, and you always know the ground truth. That's very different from most domains where people try to apply RL.

And it cuts the other way too. One of the big concerns people have with large models is that they're confident and wrong. If you pair a model with a proof assistant like Lean or with an SMT solver, the model can propose and the checker disposes. The model gets to be creative, suggest lemmas, guess invariants, pick tactics, and the symbolic engine guarantees that whatever comes out the other end is actually correct. At AWS we've seen that pattern with things like Zelkova and the work we do on verifying IAM policies and cryptographic code. The hard part was never checking a proof; it was finding it. If learned systems can do the finding, we can scale verification to problems we'd never have had the engineering hours to tackle by hand.

So I'd say: the marriage is natural, the feedback loop is clean, and I think we're going to look back on this period as when formal methods stopped being a niche activity and became something you could point at ordinary software and infrastructure at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very promising combination. In theorem proving, you often have a very large space of possible next steps. Which lemma should you try? Which case should you split on? Reinforcement learning can help guide those choices, learning which moves tend to lead to a proof.

The nice thing is that the theorem prover can check the result. The learning system can suggest something, and it can be wrong, but that doesn’t mean we accept an incorrect proof. We still require the proof to check.

So you get this interesting combination of learned intuition and rigorous reasoning. The challenge is that the reward can be quite sparse: you might take a long sequence of steps before you know whether you’ve succeeded. But there’s a really compelling opportunity there to use learning to make these tools more effective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. In theorem proving, you’re often searching an enormous space of possible steps. Reinforcement learning can help guide that search: which lemma should I try, which tactic should I apply, which direction looks promising?

The nice thing is that the theorem prover can check the result. The learning system doesn’t have to be right every time. It can suggest something, and the prover tells us whether that step is valid. So you combine the ability to learn useful strategies with a rigorous way to establish correctness.

The challenge is getting a useful learning signal. If the only reward comes when you finish a difficult proof, that can be very sparse. But I think there’s a lot of potential in learning from smaller successes and using those to tackle increasingly difficult problems.
